mappings.note: Editing task: supply the missing word in each line (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries). Pure grammatical-form work, so C-ENG3.1-LO-1 and not C-ENG4.1-LO-1 -- nothing here is about organising sentences for an audience.

Rearrange scrambled phrases into meaningful sentences using the worked example as the clue. That is organising with verbal clues (C-ENG4.1-LO-1), not choosing a grammatical form (C-ENG3.1-LO-1) -- every word is already correctly inflected.

Dialogue rewritten as a past-tense paragraph -- reported speech, i.e. tense and pronoun shift. C-ENG3.1-LO-1 over C-ENG4.2-LO-2 ('a story from dialogues') because what is graded is the backshift, not the narrative.
Same reported-speech transformation (captain/Rajeev conversation to indirect narration). Grammar LO, not the dialogue-writing LO, for the same reason.
Mother/daughter dialogue to indirect speech; the blanks test tense backshift and reporting verbs. C-ENG3.1-LO-1.
Rekha/Suresh dialogue to indirect speech. Grammar LO. (Answer text carries the 'NODIA' watermark, ignored.)
Error correction: subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun, adjective form, superlative, modal. Squarely C-ENG3.1-LO-1 rather than any writing LO -- nothing is composed.
The deliverable is a written list (languages spoken in the class) displayed on chart paper. C-ENG4.1-LO-2 names 'list' explicitly; C-ENG4.1-LO-1 would be the choice if it asked for connected prose.

Personal-preference prompt ('which language do you enjoy reading and learning in'). No LO covers speaking/writing about oneself; the goal statement does ('speak about self and experiences'). C-ENG2.2-LO-1 was rejected -- it is about reading a range of genres, not naming a preferred language.

Observation of a poster, not a text. The goal (locate details) applies but no LO does -- C-ENG2.1-LO-2 presumes a text. Stimulus is visual. Answer ends with the 'Click Here to Buy book on Amazon' advert leak.

Extract-based comprehension set (complete-the-reason, true/false, choose the option, name the feeling). Answering questions on a given text, so C-ENG1.1-LO-1; the individual sub-items are answerable from the extract, so not the critical-thinking branch.

Asks why the writer opens with detailed nature description -- authorial craft, reading beyond the literal. Under CG-ENG2 via C-ENG2.1-LO-2, not C-ENG1.1-LO-1, because the answer is nowhere in the text.
How the River knew about Jahnavi -- the answer is a stated detail ('every day, well, almost every day'). Retrieval, so C-ENG1.1-LO-1, not the inference branch.
Explicitly 'what can you infer' about Jahnavi and about village schooling. Reading between the lines, so the CG-ENG2 branch rather than C-ENG1.1-LO-1.
Dream, its importance, and the reason -- all stated in the text (the 'many whys'). Retrieval, C-ENG1.1-LO-1.
'Do you think the river can help her? How?' -- an evaluative judgement supported from the text. CG-ENG2 branch, not plain retrieval.
Table to be completed by pairing Jahnavi's questions with the River's answers -- locating details. C-ENG1.1-LO-1 rather than C-ENG4.1-LO-1; no continuous writing is asked for.

Stem is corrupted -- a glossary entry for 'palanquin' is prepended to the real task. The task that survives is a personal choice of boat plus a drawing; that is speaking about self/preference, for which only the goal statement fits. No LO covers drawing.
Why the River laughed -- the reason is given in the text (lizards, snakes, trains). Retrieval, not inference.
'Why should Jahnavi follow the advice?' asks the reader to weigh it, which the text never states. CG-ENG2 branch.
How the Jahnavi/River conversation makes the story appealing -- a judgement about narrative technique. CG-ENG2 branch, not C-ENG1.1-LO-1.
Central message of the story. CG-ENG2 is the goal about the central idea; C-ENG2.1-LO-2 is its response-to-text LO. Not retrieval.

Corrupted stem -- the answer key of the preceding prepositions exercise ('on, 2. outside, 3. to...') is prepended to a listening task (circle the words the five speakers use). Listening comprehension has no LO of its own; CG-ENG1 is the listening goal.

Observe nature, then write a descriptive paragraph on colours, textures and movement. C-ENG4.2-LO-1 names descriptions with environmental sensitivity; C-ENG4.1-LO-1 would understate it as mere sentence ordering.

A crossword clue defining 'yacht' by meaning and rhyme -- word-meaning/reference work, so C-ENG2.2-LO-2 rather than C-ENG3.1-LO-1 (no grammatical form is at issue). Note the stored answer belongs to the NEXT exercise (prepositions), not to this clue.
Inference from the poster image ('why do the girls look happy'). Visual stimulus, so the text-bound LOs do not apply; cited at goal level.
Relates 'dignity' to 'happiness' by reading the poster slogan. Beyond-the-text reasoning off a visual; goal level for the same reason as the sibling poster items.

'How does a nation prosper when its daughters are happy' -- goes entirely beyond the stimulus. CG-ENG2's 'go beyond the text' clause; C-ENG4.2-LO-1 was rejected because no description or narrative is asked for.
Parents' reaction to the teacher's visit -- stated in the text. Retrieval.
What Jahnavi decided to do when grown up -- stated (become a teacher, go house to house). Retrieval.
The River's promise of more ship stories -- a stated detail. Retrieval, not the inference branch, although the answer adds a gloss.
List of things Jahnavi wanted to learn -- all enumerated in the text. Retrieval.

'Describe Jahnavi's background and early dream' -- an extended written answer assembled from stated details. C-ENG1.1-LO-1 ('orally and in writing'), not a C-ENG4 writing LO, since nothing original is composed.
How the River first spoke to her -- quotable detail. Retrieval.
The River's advice about school -- quoted in the text. Retrieval.
How she finally got to school -- a sequence of stated events. Retrieval; sequencing alone does not make it inference.
How the mother's view changed -- both positions are stated, the reader only contrasts them. Retrieval. (Answer truncated mid-sentence by the 'NODIA' watermark.)
MCQ, what Jahnavi was doing when she heard the voice. Single stated detail.
MCQ on her reaction at the end of the story -- named in the closing lines. Retrieval.
MCQ, what the River says she shouldn't be ('afraid'). Quoted detail.
MCQ on the lizard's colour -- a single descriptive detail. Retrieval.
MCQ on the river's destination (the sea). Stated detail.
MCQ on where Jahnavi stood while listening to the teacher. Stated detail.
MCQ naming the central character. Retrieval, not a craft question.
Unpacks the metaphor 'an arrow of blue in the sunlight' -- figurative language and what it suggests. CG-ENG2 branch; nothing literal is being retrieved.
'What can you infer about her family's priorities' from an unfinished thought. Explicit inference, CG-ENG2 branch.
Extract with four sub-questions, each answerable from the printed lines (voice type, 'startled', true/false, which creatures ruled out). Retrieval.
Where the family lived -- one-line stated fact.
Her big dream -- one-line stated fact. Retrieval.
Who startled her -- stated. Retrieval.
What the mother said when she was five ('too small, baby') -- quoted. Retrieval.
Brother's real name (Gopi) -- stated. Retrieval.
The River's suggested method ('slip along one morning and sit there') -- quoted. Retrieval.
Which animal came to the river's edge -- stated detail.
The father's habit when worried (scratched his cheek) -- stated detail.
Who fell asleep on her shoulder (Appu) -- stated detail.
What she wanted to become -- stated. Retrieval.
Describe the family and where they lived -- assembled from stated details, so retrieval in writing rather than a composition LO.
Dream plus the stated obstacles (too small, minding brothers). Retrieval; the causal link is given in the text.
